Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

text:
An investigation by Reuters has revealed a major lapse in India’s internet censorship mechanism, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) ordered the blocking of 129 betting websites based on forged orders from the Rajasthan and Allahabad High Courts.
Despite rules requiring certified copies of judicial orders, the government acted on fake documents one of which even contained a QR code leading to an unrelated webpage without verifying them with the courts. The Allahabad High Court has since confirmed the case never existed and filed a police complaint.
While targeting illegal betting platforms is lawful, bypassing verification checks sets a dangerous precedent for digital rights and press freedom. If forged documents can trigger state censorship machinery today, independent journalism and free speech could be next. Who is accountable when official safeguards fail?

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

@Meta ,

You built platforms that hold our memories, our businesses, our friendships, our work. Then you handed the keys to AI and walked away.

Accounts on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp are being disabled or suspended overnight by automated systems. No clear reason. No warning. No human in the loop. Just a bot decision that can erase years of life in seconds.

Sometimes you send an email later saying “we made a mistake, you can use the account again.” Then nothing changes. The account stays locked. Or worse while it’s locked in appeal, it gets compromised. Unauthorized recovery numbers appear. Hidden apps show up. Codes stop working. And the person who built that account for a decade is left staring at recovery screens that keep changing.

No acknowledgment of what the user went through while they were locked out  the panic, the lost clients, the family photos they couldn’t reach, the nights spent arguing with a chatbot that loops forever.

This is not a rare glitch anymore. It’s a pattern. AI is deciding who gets to keep their digital life, and when it gets it wrong, there is almost no path to a real human.

Meta Verified users, people who filed cybercrime complaints, people who used the official Grievance Officer process under the IT Rules many of them are still waiting. The support system points them back to the same AI that caused the problem.

When GST dues outlive the business: what ICAI's updated handbook says about directors, partners, buyers and heirs

When a GST demand cannot be collected from the business, the department looks for someone else to pay it. Sections 85 to 94 of the CGST Act decide who that someone is. ICAI's GST and Indirect Taxes Committee has just released the second edition of its handbook on these provisions, and it is a good prompt to check where your clients stand.

The Handbook on Liability to Pay in Certain Cases under GST, second edition, carries a preface dated October 2026 and states the law as at 30 September 2026. The first edition was published in 2020.

Why this matters now

Recovery has moved from returns to people. As adjudication and appeal backlogs clear, and GSTAT benches decide more cases, confirmed demands against closed, sold or struck-off businesses are turning into notices against directors, partners, buyers of businesses and heirs. Many clients who receive such a notice did not know the liability could follow them.

Transfer of business: section 85

Where a taxable person transfers the business, in whole or in part, by sale, gift, lease, leave and licence, hire or any other manner, the transferor and the transferee are jointly and severally liable for tax, interest and penalty due up to the date of transfer. It does not matter whether the amount was determined before the transfer or afterwards. After the transfer, the transferee is liable for its own supplies and must amend its registration.

The handbook makes a distinction that matters in practice. A transfer of shares alone is not a transfer of business. Buying individual assets is not necessarily a transfer of business either. It cites JR Metal Chennai Ltd v Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax, decided by the Andhra Pradesh High Court on 8 May 2024, where a buyer of plant, land and building argued that it had not taken over the business. The court treated the question as one of fact and sent the party to its appellate remedy. The lesson for any acquirer is that the label on the deed does not settle the question. The substance of what was taken over does.

The handbook also reminds readers that transfer of a going concern, as a whole or an independent part, is exempt under Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28 June 2017, and that Circular 96/15/2019-GST dated 28 March 2019 treats transfer on the death of a sole proprietor as a transfer of ownership for registration and credit purposes.

Amalgamation: section 87

Where companies amalgamate under a court or tribunal order with an earlier appointed date, supplies between them during the interim period are taxable, and the companies are treated as distinct until the date of the order. Their registrations are cancelled from that date. The handbook refers to recent decisions, including Kanakia Spaces Realty v Union of India (Bombay High Court, 24 June 2026), where a notice issued in the name of a company that had ceased to exist on amalgamation was held to be void. The point for practitioners is simple: tell the department about the order, and make sure notices are issued to the right entity.

Liquidation: section 88

A liquidator must inform the Commissioner of the appointment within thirty days. The Commissioner then has three months to tell the liquidator how much should be set aside for tax, interest and penalty. Where a private company is wound up and dues cannot be recovered, every person who was a director during the relevant period is jointly and severally liable, unless the director proves that the failure cannot be attributed to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty. Section 88 operates subject to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

Directors of private companies: section 89

This is the provision that worries clients most. Notwithstanding the Companies Act, 2013, where dues of a private company for any period cannot be recovered, every person who was a director during that period is jointly and severally liable. The same escape route applies: the director must prove that non-recovery cannot be attributed to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part. If the private company is converted into a public company, the provision does not apply to dues for the private-company period where recovery had already failed, though personal penalties remain recoverable.

Two things follow. The burden is on the director, not the department. And liability turns on who was a director during the period of supply, not who is a director when the notice arrives. A director who resigned in 2021 is not safe for dues of 2019.

Partners: section 90

A firm and each of its partners are jointly and severally liable for the firm's tax, interest and penalty, whatever the partnership deed says. A retiring partner remains liable for dues up to the date of retirement, determined or not. The trap is the intimation. If the partner or the firm does not inform the Commissioner in writing within one month of retirement, the liability continues until the intimation is received. There is no gross-neglect defence for partners.

Death and other cases: section 93

If a business continues after the owner's death, the legal representative or the person carrying it on is liable for dues. If the business is discontinued, the legal representative is liable only to the extent of the estate. Similar rules apply on partition of an HUF or AOP, dissolution of a firm and termination of a guardianship or trust. Each operates subject to the IBC.

The remaining sections cover agents and principals (section 86), guardians, trustees and courts of wards (sections 91 and 92) and certain other cases (section 94). The handbook deals with each.

My reading

Most of these liabilities are avoidable with paperwork done on time. Retiring partners forget the one-month intimation. Buyers of running businesses skip a GST due diligence because the price is attractive. Directors of family private companies sign nothing about compliance and then struggle to show they were not negligent. A liquidator misses the thirty-day intimation and takes on avoidable risk.

The section 89 defence deserves preparation, not improvisation. A non-executive or nominee director should be able to show what was delegated, to whom, what reports were received and what was done when problems surfaced. Board minutes noting GST compliance status, and written delegation to a named officer, are the evidence that later carries the burden.

On acquisitions, I would treat GST exposure like any other contingent liability. Pull the GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-9 history, check pending SCNs and orders on the portal, and ask for an indemnity backed by an escrow or retention where the risk is real. Joint and several liability means the department can recover from the buyer first.

Action points

1. For every partner retirement, send a written intimation to the jurisdictional officer within one month and keep the acknowledgement.

2. Run a GST due diligence before buying any running business or business unit: returns, ledgers, notices and pending appeals.

3. Draft business transfer agreements with clear allocation of pre-transfer GST dues, indemnities and a retention or escrow.

4. In private companies, record GST compliance in board minutes and document delegation to a named officer.

5. On amalgamation, file the order with the department promptly and update registrations from the order date.

6. Liquidators must intimate the Commissioner within thirty days of appointment.

7. On a proprietor's death, decide quickly whether the business will continue, because the heir's exposure differs sharply between the two cases.

GST dues do not die with the business. They move to the people who were nearest to it, unless the paperwork was done when it mattered.

This is general information, not advice. Check the provisions and your facts before acting.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

When GST dues outlive the business: what ICAI's updated handbook says about directors, partners, buyers and heirs

When a GST demand cannot be collected from the business, the department looks for someone else to pay it. Sections 85 to 94 of the CGST Act decide who that someone is. ICAI's GST and Indirect Taxes Committee has just released the second edition of its handbook on these provisions, and it is a good prompt to check where your clients stand.

The Handbook on Liability to Pay in Certain Cases under GST, second edition, carries a preface dated October 2026 and states the law as at 30 September 2026. The first edition was published in 2020.

Why this matters now

Recovery has moved from returns to people. As adjudication and appeal backlogs clear, and GSTAT benches decide more cases, confirmed demands against closed, sold or struck-off businesses are turning into notices against directors, partners, buyers of businesses and heirs. Many clients who receive such a notice did not know the liability could follow them.

Transfer of business: section 85

Where a taxable person transfers the business, in whole or in part, by sale, gift, lease, leave and licence, hire or any other manner, the transferor and the transferee are jointly and severally liable for tax, interest and penalty due up to the date of transfer. It does not matter whether the amount was determined before the transfer or afterwards. After the transfer, the transferee is liable for its own supplies and must amend its registration.

The handbook makes a distinction that matters in practice. A transfer of shares alone is not a transfer of business. Buying individual assets is not necessarily a transfer of business either. It cites JR Metal Chennai Ltd v Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax, decided by the Andhra Pradesh High Court on 8 May 2024, where a buyer of plant, land and building argued that it had not taken over the business. The court treated the question as one of fact and sent the party to its appellate remedy. The lesson for any acquirer is that the label on the deed does not settle the question. The substance of what was taken over does.

The handbook also reminds readers that transfer of a going concern, as a whole or an independent part, is exempt under Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28 June 2017, and that Circular 96/15/2019-GST dated 28 March 2019 treats transfer on the death of a sole proprietor as a transfer of ownership for registration and credit purposes.

Amalgamation: section 87

Where companies amalgamate under a court or tribunal order with an earlier appointed date, supplies between them during the interim period are taxable, and the companies are treated as distinct until the date of the order. Their registrations are cancelled from that date. The handbook refers to recent decisions, including Kanakia Spaces Realty v Union of India (Bombay High Court, 24 June 2026), where a notice issued in the name of a company that had ceased to exist on amalgamation was held to be void. The point for practitioners is simple: tell the department about the order, and make sure notices are issued to the right entity.

Liquidation: section 88

A liquidator must inform the Commissioner of the appointment within thirty days. The Commissioner then has three months to tell the liquidator how much should be set aside for tax, interest and penalty. Where a private company is wound up and dues cannot be recovered, every person who was a director during the relevant period is jointly and severally liable, unless the director proves that the failure cannot be attributed to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty. Section 88 operates subject to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

Directors of private companies: section 89

This is the provision that worries clients most. Notwithstanding the Companies Act, 2013, where dues of a private company for any period cannot be recovered, every person who was a director during that period is jointly and severally liable. The same escape route applies: the director must prove that non-recovery cannot be attributed to gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part. If the private company is converted into a public company, the provision does not apply to dues for the private-company period where recovery had already failed, though personal penalties remain recoverable.

Two things follow. The burden is on the director, not the department. And liability turns on who was a director during the period of supply, not who is a director when the notice arrives. A director who resigned in 2021 is not safe for dues of 2019.

Partners: section 90

A firm and each of its partners are jointly and severally liable for the firm's tax, interest and penalty, whatever the partnership deed says. A retiring partner remains liable for dues up to the date of retirement, determined or not. The trap is the intimation. If the partner or the firm does not inform the Commissioner in writing within one month of retirement, the liability continues until the intimation is received. There is no gross-neglect defence for partners.

Death and other cases: section 93

If a business continues after the owner's death, the legal representative or the person carrying it on is liable for dues. If the business is discontinued, the legal representative is liable only to the extent of the estate. Similar rules apply on partition of an HUF or AOP, dissolution of a firm and termination of a guardianship or trust. Each operates subject to the IBC.

The remaining sections cover agents and principals (section 86), guardians, trustees and courts of wards (sections 91 and 92) and certain other cases (section 94). The handbook deals with each.

My reading

Most of these liabilities are avoidable with paperwork done on time. Retiring partners forget the one-month intimation. Buyers of running businesses skip a GST due diligence because the price is attractive. Directors of family private companies sign nothing about compliance and then struggle to show they were not negligent. A liquidator misses the thirty-day intimation and takes on avoidable risk.

The section 89 defence deserves preparation, not improvisation. A non-executive or nominee director should be able to show what was delegated, to whom, what reports were received and what was done when problems surfaced. Board minutes noting GST compliance status, and written delegation to a named officer, are the evidence that later carries the burden.

On acquisitions, I would treat GST exposure like any other contingent liability. Pull the GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-9 history, check pending SCNs and orders on the portal, and ask for an indemnity backed by an escrow or retention where the risk is real. Joint and several liability means the department can recover from the buyer first.

Action points

1. For every partner retirement, send a written intimation to the jurisdictional officer within one month and keep the acknowledgement.

2. Run a GST due diligence before buying any running business or business unit: returns, ledgers, notices and pending appeals.

3. Draft business transfer agreements with clear allocation of pre-transfer GST dues, indemnities and a retention or escrow.

4. In private companies, record GST compliance in board minutes and document delegation to a named officer.

5. On amalgamation, file the order with the department promptly and update registrations from the order date.

6. Liquidators must intimate the Commissioner within thirty days of appointment.

7. On a proprietor's death, decide quickly whether the business will continue, because the heir's exposure differs sharply between the two cases.

GST dues do not die with the business. They move to the people who were nearest to it, unless the paperwork was done when it mattered.

This is general information, not advice. Check the provisions and your facts before acting.

**The Unrestricted Internet Free Speech Act**  
*(The strongest practicable statutory protection of speech consistent with negative liberty and the non-aggression principle)*

**Section 1. Absolute Protection**  
Congress, the States, and every political subdivision, agency, official, or instrumentality thereof shall make no law, issue no rule, enter no order, impose no tax, license, or prior restraint, and take no action abridging the freedom of speech, of the press, or of expression on the internet or any electronic network.  

This protection is absolute as to content and viewpoint. It extends to every form of expression—words, images, video, audio, code, data, memes, satire, fiction, opinion, commercial speech, political speech, religious speech, scientific claims, false statements, offensive statements, and all other communicative acts—except only those categories that constitute initiated force or fraud under longstanding principles: true threats of imminent violence directed at a specific person, speech integral to criminal conduct (such as solicitation of a specific crime), and defamation proven by actual malice under the strictest common-law standards.

**Section 2. No Government Censorship or Compulsion**  
No public official or entity may:  
(a) remove, throttle, label, demonetize, deplatform, shadow-ban, or otherwise suppress any internet speech on the basis of its content or viewpoint;  
(b) compel any person, platform, or intermediary to speak, to host speech, to affirm any proposition, or to disclose the identity of a speaker except pursuant to a specific judicial warrant supported by probable cause of a completed crime involving force or fraud;  
(c) impose civil or criminal liability on any speaker, publisher, platform, or intermediary for the content of third-party speech;  
(d) fund, incentivize, or pressure private parties to censor speech that the government itself could not prohibit.

**Section 3. Intermediary Freedom and Immunity**  
Interactive computer services, platforms, hosts, and infrastructure providers possess the same pre-political rights of property, association, and editorial discretion as any other private owner. They may include, exclude, moderate, or refuse speech on their own property for any reason or no reason.  

They shall not be treated as publishers or speakers of third-party content and shall enjoy absolute immunity from liability arising from the speech of others or from their decisions to host or remove speech, except where they themselves originate speech that constitutes force or fraud. No law shall condition this immunity on any content-moderation practice, “neutrality” requirement, or government-approved standard.

**Section 4. Preemption and Supremacy**  
This Act preempts and supersedes any conflicting federal, state, or local statute, regulation, common-law rule, or executive action to the extent it abridges internet speech. International agreements and foreign judgments shall not be enforced within the United States if they would punish speech protected by this Act.  

Any person whose speech is abridged by government action in violation of this Act may bring suit for injunctive relief, declaratory relief, actual damages, statutory damages of not less than $100,000 per violation, and attorney’s fees. Qualified immunity is abolished for claims arising under this Act. Prevailing plaintiffs shall recover costs as of right.

**Section 5. Construction**  
This Act shall be construed in favor of maximum protection for speech and against any claimed governmental interest in suppressing expression. Ambiguities are resolved for the speaker. The internet is recognized as a domain in which the pre-political right of free speech is especially broad because exit, counter-speech, and voluntary association remain fully available.  

No emergency, public-health claim, national-security assertion, or allegation of “harm,” “misinformation,” “hate,” or “safety” shall justify any abridgment prohibited by this Act.

**Section 6. Severability and Non-Delegation**  
If any provision is held invalid, the remainder continues in force at full strength. No agency may issue rules implementing this Act that narrow its protections; any such attempt is void.

Examine SECO's specific penalty thresholds for Swiss commodity traders caught breaching secondary Iran sanctions. (1)

In Switzerland, the enforcement of international trade restrictions and asset freezes is legally governed by the Federal Act on the Implementation of International Sanctions (Embargo Act, EmbA). Under this statutory framework, the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) operates as the primary investigating, prosecuting, and adjudicating authority for sanctions infractions. 

https://t.co/2DKbQDM2ly

For Swiss-registered commodity traders navigating complex energy and maritime networks, SECO applies distinct criminal penalty thresholds based on the intent, negligence, and structural severity of the violation:

https://t.co/MFTBKG8VN4

1. Statutory Criminal Penalty Thresholds under the EmbA

Swiss law does not utilize a separate civil penalty regime for trade violations; all sanctions breaches are treated as administrative criminal offenses governed by the Federal Act on Administrative Criminal Law (ACL):

https://t.co/2DKbQDM2ly

•Intentional (Wilful) Violations (Art. 9, Para. 1): If a commodity trading desk knowingly bypasses restrictions—such as fabricating end-user certificates or utilizing illicit maritime routes to facilitate barred trades—individuals can face up to 1 year of imprisonment or a substantial monetary penalty.

https://t.co/IUmO0ZHlU2

•Serious and Aggravated Cases (Art. 9, Para. 2): For major corporate infractions, structural evasion, or repetitive illicit trade operations, the penalty threshold escalates significantly to up to 5 years of custodial imprisonment combined with statutory fines of up to CHF 1 million. 

https://t.co/w44hl0IM8c

•Negligent Breaches (Art. 9, Para. 3): If a firm fails to properly audit its supply chains or verify a third-party intermediary, resulting in an inadvertent breach, the infraction is penalized with a fine of up to CHF 100,000. 

https://t.co/IUmO0ZHlU2

2. Violations of Information and Disclosure Requests (Art. 10)

During an active investigation or routine audit of a Geneva- or Zug-based trading desk, SECO holds the legal power to demand internal shipping manifests, bank clearing receipts, and communications:

Can someone impersonate a police officer,
to trigger the removal of social media accounts?

X told the Delhi High Court that it received purported takedown notices, allegedly issued in the name of a senior Delhi Police officer.

Targeting the accounts of Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and SFLC.

The twist? 
X’s investigation reportedly found the notices were FAKE!

Who was behind this?. 1/2

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Deepfake scams are no longer a freak event. They have a price tag.

On November 10, 2026, the VPN and security company Surfshark published a study, "Deepfakes cost billions as incidents hit 114 countries." It counted 2,430 deepfake incidents in news reports from January 2020 through September 2026, compiled from the AI Incident Database, Resemble AI and the OECD. In Surfshark's words, "nearly 90% of all incidents occurred from 2024 onwards."

The same study estimates $3.91 billion in deepfake-enabled fraud losses, with 98% of that total also occurring from 2024 onwards. Combined reported losses for 2020 through 2023 were $83 million. They jumped to $335 million in 2024, then reached a record $2.52 billion in 2025. Through the first three quarters of 2026, losses were already $972 million. Incident counts in those same 2026 quarters reached 809, up 24% from 651 in the same period of 2025. The full-year record in 2025 was 970. With those 809 incidents already documented, Surfshark said 2026 "is on pace to set a new record."

Investment scams that use deepfakes of celebrities and public figures caused $1.75 billion — 45% of the $3.91 billion — across 254 of the 768 fraud incidents in the dataset.

Surfshark recorded incidents in 114 countries. The United States led with 787, followed by India (246), the United Kingdom (141), China (111), Brazil (79) and South Korea (76).

Posts 2–5 cover where these scams find you: the social feed, the live video call, the cloned-voice phone call, and a fake CEO stock-tip video. Post 6 is the checklist; post 7 recaps the limits of a news-based count. 🧵

5. The solution checklist — verify off the clip.

My recommended response to a face or voice that asks you to move money or invest:

The immediate fix:

1. Do not invest, send money or share account details because a celebrity or official appears to be speaking in a video.
2. Leave the clip or call and verify the claim through an official website, app or phone number you already have, not a link or number supplied in the message.
3. Use a call-back rule, and agree on a family safe word for any urgent money request.
4. Never move money, shares or crypto on a video call alone, even if the face looks right and someone else on the call appears to confirm it.
5. If a stock tip points you to WhatsApp, Telegram or a private group, treat that as a warning, not a bonus channel.

Tomas Stamulis, Chief Security Officer at Surfshark, put the practical rule this way: "Seeing or hearing someone is no longer enough to know it’s really them."

6. The recap — $3.91 billion, counted from the news.

Surfshark's November 10, 2026 study is the source of the figures in this thread: 2,430 incidents, $3.91 billion in estimated losses, and a clear channel split in the 768 fraud cases.

Lines worth keeping:

"nearly 90% of all incidents occurred from 2024 onwards"

"Social media was the primary first-contact channel for spreading deepfake-related fraud, accounting for 57% of recorded cases (438 of 768) and $2.16 billion in financial losses (55% of the total)."

"Seeing or hearing someone is no longer enough to know it’s really them."

One honest caveat: Surfshark counted only incidents covered in news reports, drawing on the AI Incident Database, Resemble AI and the OECD, so the true totals are likely higher, and country rankings partly reflect where cases get reported. A multi-country incident is counted once in the global total and in each affected country. Surfshark is also a company that sells a VPN and other security products. The $972 million figure is for the first three quarters of 2026, not the year through November.

TRANSCRIPT
A lawsuit could constrain new AI models if a court grants the restrictions sought by four nonprofits. The groups allege public-safety harms and violations of California unfair-competition law, asking a San Francisco court to freeze development or deployment at five AI firms. The defendants named are Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen and the Alliance for Secure AI. No court has ruled on the allegations, and the requested freeze is not an existing ban.

AI-generated candidate impersonations can manipulate the information voters see. The European Commission’s proposed election guidance asks very large platforms and search engines to label deepfakes clearly, keep those labels attached when shared, and swiftly remove illegal candidate deepfakes. It also proposes testing recommendation algorithms for manipulation before national elections and publishing post-election risk reports. The draft consultation opened November tenth and closes November twenty-third. These are proposed guidelines under the Digital Services Act, not new binding rules, and the draft does not request deletion of lawful content.

Small AI developers need a way to test systems with regulatory supervision before putting them on the market. The European Commission has adopted binding common procedures for AI testing sandboxes, giving small businesses and start-ups priority and free regulatory guidance, apart from exceptional costs. Selection decisions normally come within three months of a complete application or call deadline. The regulation was adopted November tenth. Participation provides written proof and an exit report documenting the testing, not certification that the product complies. Member states must establish at least one sandbox by August second, twenty twenty-seven.

Calling restaurants or service providers is a practical task AI agents can take on for people. Meta says Muse can place calls to American businesses, citing cable companies, motor-vehicle departments and restaurants as examples. The feature previously served selected early adopters. It is now available to paid subscribers in the United States, an expansion of access rather than the first introduction of calling. TechCrunch reports that subscriptions start at twenty dollars a month; the report does not provide independent success-rate or business-acceptance figures.

AI-written clinical notes require checks before becoming part of a patient’s record. EkaCare says India’s National Health Authority selected it for an AI scribe that listens to consultations and creates structured notes in more than fifteen Indian languages, including mixed-language conversations. A verified doctor must review, edit if necessary, and approve every note before linkage to the patient account. The company also open-sourced Lipi, its related conversation-to-notes AI scribe framework, which individuals and organizations can run on their own infrastructure. The clinical system is designed for authority-controlled infrastructure and hospital-software integration; the announcement establishes neither national rollout nor measured clinical gains.

Using AI in education raises a concrete question: does a tool preserve the learner’s chances to practice skills and build human relationships? Harvard’s Compass Collaborative includes an AI Guidance by Age matrix that tailors recommendations to learner age, developmental domain and the user’s role. Researchers drew on more than five thousand education, psychology and development studies, much of it from before generative AI. The initiative launched November tenth. The matrix is an evolving advisory resource with assessment considerations and possible benefits or harms, while direct evidence of AI’s learning effects remains limited. It does not prove that a particular AI tool improves learning.

An AI-authorship accusation put a winning writer’s work and literary award under scrutiny. The Guardian reports that the Pangram detector rated the story as almost entirely AI-generated, which the author denied. The Caine Prize board interviewed the author, judges and publisher and commissioned independent metadata analysis of draft documents. The board found no evidence that generative AI produced the story and confirmed that the award stands. That is the prize’s review finding, not scientific validation of AI detectors. The prize also plans AI declarations for twenty twenty-seven submissions and shortlisted writers, judge guidance and a process for reviewing future concerns.

SpaceX has outlined five contingency landing options for Starship Flight 15 as it prepares for the ship’s first tower-catch attempt at Starbase

This visualization shows how the mission can change course if the vehicle or tower does not meet the conditions required for a safe return:

1. Indian Ocean — after ascent
If the orbital insertion burn is skipped, Starship remains on its suborbital trajectory and reenters over a predetermined area of the Indian Ocean

2. North of Hawaii — early in the mission
If the flight needs to end shortly after reaching orbit, Starship returns to a designated area of the Pacific north of Hawaii

3. Off Chile — mid-mission
A separate return opportunity allows Starship to land in the eastern Pacific, far off the coast of Chile

4. Gulf offshore — catch contingency
If the tower catch is called off before final approach, Starship has an offshore landing option in the Gulf instead of proceeding with the catch

5. North of Hawaii — late in the mission
If the planned deorbit burn is skipped, Starship completes another orbit before returning to the Pacific north of Hawaii

The objective is to bring Starship home. The flight plan builds in alternatives throughout the journey, with continuous vehicle-health checks determining when to proceed

An ambitious mission, backed by carefully planned options from ascent to final approach

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Now that you've gone through the documentation and the police have picked up the investigation, the real question you should ask is how is this possible. 

How can your information be associated with another individual then duplicated to AT LEAST 600 different search sites. It's easier to manipulate than you suspect. Unfortunately, I had to become an expert when attempting to clear my name. 

The companies get data from mulitples sources: address change database from the USPS, DMV records, utility records and a major one is insurance data bases. 

Theoreticallly, if I knew you had a similar name to someone with a questionable history, I can just spam auto insurance sign ups with that individual and use your address or phone number. After about a good month that person shows as a 'possible match'. Get mail sent from the other individual's name to an address matching yours and that's another data point. 

In my case, he was spamming and harassing me by signing me up for insurance quotes. The other individual, Jeremy LEE Williams (a white male) began appearing on my searches. He had multiple addresses in SC. Once the slander began, I was in fear of my address leaking so I checked everyday. The house I stay in was previously a rental for college students since Wake Forest is right down the road. The incentives were the area and the fact that utilities were included. I paid way more than I normally would have for a comparible spot but the utilities kind of made it even. That saved me while being stalked. But it didn't save the narrative he created on the internet. 

When I did suppression requests the identities then became merged instead of just removing MY information. When you searched for my name, age and a previous address it showed the search as a verified match. Then my actual information was listed with his, my former addresses, some of my actual associates, with his addresses and criminal history as well. So now when they searched, they had ammo. This man had meth, domestic violence and about 5 other heinous charges listed. Now they belong to me....on the internet.

This was replicated on and on. At one point it was over 600 sites. I used data removal services. They could only get rid of the ones in which my contact information matched. The ones where HIS phone number and email were required for verification were left. BBB helped me remove some. I honestly had to lie and say I was him to remove the association. I reached out to Lexis Nexis since they are an aggregator. No dice. Technically it was his record, with mine being attached even though it was populating as a verified match. 

This was hell. I kept trying. Even the suppressions popped backed up. One on https://t.co/E0j7yv9EWp had 5 different Jeremy Williams's listed with MY birthdate. I provided screen recordings of all of this. They allowed the suppression to go through after I filed a police report. 1 down 600 plus to go. 

I don't know if he was smart enough to know what he was doing, but targeting me for spam and using addresses that he thought were mine and my REAL name and phone number caused the systems to create matching data points with the white Jeremy. 

I went one by one of the charges of this individual and matched his case numbers with his actual arrest data and mugshots. I screen recording this as well. 

Answers should be brought on how this is possible. Before I finally gave up, I reached out to Minc Law.  I know the whole story sounded convoluted. But once I responded with actual evidence it made sense. I never lost a job opportunity because of these. Jobs use real screening and are governed by the FCRA. The people search sites are not. I also learned that you are governed by arbitration in case you do sue them, the amount is already set. So matter what damage is caused, even if your life is ruined they have no liability. 

This is why you should care about a random individual that endured every kind of humilitation possible. The crime was taking care of my mother and being lied on by a sociopath.

There is no real pathway to justice for a normal person. I've been lied on for almost 3 years. Yes, 3. 

Everybody asked why I didn't respond. The answer is that I shouldn't have had to. I shouldn't have to open this up to an even bigger audience to give the allegations more credibility. No job wants their Project Manager associated with any of the things he put on me. No supposedly reputable search site should validate it either. 

@FTC @NCAGO @SCAttyGenOffice @CFPB @EPICprivacy @LexisNexis

This is legit free money for anyone who takes on this case. I have laid out all evidence. I just want my name restored even if I'm not able to see it.

Rachel Clayton: “india’s government is facing fresh questions about press freedom after dozens of journalists were detained while covering youth-led protests. reporters in the capital of new delhi fear the crackdown is part of a wider effort to control what indians see and hear. thousands came to protest, but it was those who came to report. that became the story. the committee to protect journalists says at least 43 reporters were detained while covering this month’s rallies, the vast majority in new delhi. shoaib daniyal has worked for the online newspaper scroll for over a decade.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “there was a checkpoint right outside my house. i spoke to a cop, i asked him about the protest. he became suspicious, he became angry, he said i’m going to detain you. he detained me.”

Rachel Clayton: “shoaib filmed his detention.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “why have you detained me?”

Officer: “you are wasting your time as well as mine.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “for what? what did i do?”

Rachel Clayton: “he says officers offered to release him if he wiped his phone. delete it, the officer tells him. no, he says.”

Shoaib Daniyal: “he didn’t know what to do with me, so he kind of drove me around for almost an hour and a half. eventually, i think they kind of tired themselves out and they did let me go. like, literally anyone could be just picked up and put on the bus. there seems to be no method to segregate people who may genuinely be coming in the way of police work to people who were simply there to report.”

Rachel Clayton: “police are allowed to detain anyone without a warrant under the country’s preventive detention laws, but officers must have a reasonable suspicion the person is going to commit a crime. delhi police claim they could not distinguish between traditional media and protesters filming on their phone. the latest round of demonstrations erupted over india’s election commission. protesters accused commissioner gyanesh kumar of removing millions of names from voter rolls to benefit the ruling bjp government. it comes three months after mass demonstrations forced out india’s education minister, which took everyone, including the government, by surprise.”

Former NDTV journalist: “and i think this was the response of a wounded regime, that they now wanted to hit back. they wanted to stamp out the protests using extraordinary force. and i think silencing or trying to intimidate the media in these new ways is part of that response.”

Rachel Clayton: “where do you see things pointing? he worked for ndtv for 30 years. the network won multiple awards for being india’s most trusted news brand. he resigned in 2022 when businessman gautam adani took over. the billionaire had a close relationship with the prime minister, and journalists raised concerns about editorial independence.”

Former NDTV journalist: “we’ve seen this growing pattern of the gradual takeover of media companies by corporates that are seen as close to the regime. and you also have seen separately media companies on their own flipping. so when that takeover news came, it was kind of a sign that the sort of clock had started ticking. we call them the godi media, meaning lapdog media. what is this dangerous anti-democratic ecosystem that’s being built in this country? entire swaths of particularly tv media have been brought to heel, have turned into propagandists for the government.”

Rachel Clayton: “since narendra modi took power in 2014, the majority of india’s most popular networks have been bought by corporate businesses, politicians, or people with close ties to the government. social media had begun breaking that control. ramit verma creates and publishes political satire for a large online following. he was also detained, covering recent protests. india’s government has tightened its grip on internet freedom and regularly orders social media companies to remove posts and even whole accounts.”

Ramit Verma: “it happened so much that i don’t even remember the last post that got taken down, but it’s become the norm in india right now. it’s become the norm for your posts to get taken down at any point without any explanation.”

text:
X tells Delhi High Court that the notices attributed to Delhi Police were sent by an imposter.

On 29 October 2026, Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Centre (SFLC), received a legal notice from an individual identifying themselves as Advocate Gaurav Tiwari, claiming to be acting on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).

The notice demanded that they stop documenting government content restrictions, opposing blocking directions and publishing details of geo-blocked content in India. It also asked for written confirmation within seven days that we would comply.

A second notice followed on 1 November, referring to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad (ABAP), complaints in different states and requests to block their social media accounts.

On 3 November, X forwarded takedown requests purportedly submitted by the Delhi Police. These included requests targeting the accounts of IFF, SFLC and GeoBlockedIndia, along with several individual posts and posts by other users.
The requests cited alleged defamation under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), among other grounds.

However, questions about the authenticity of these requests continued. SFLC attempted to verify them with the Delhi Police, but its communications to the email address mentioned in the notices were returned as undeliverable. The organisations also approached the Delhi Police for clarification.

On 5 November, IFF and SFLC approached the Delhi High Court challenging the notices.

On 6 November, X told the Delhi High Court that the notices attributed to Delhi Police were sent by an imposter, not the Delhi Police.

X informed the Court that it had conducted an internal investigation, found that the notices were sent by an imposter, and filed a complaint with Delhi Police.

X also confirmed that the accounts of IFF and SFLC would not be taken down. Following this submission, the Delhi High Court disposed of their petitions.

Separately, a Scroll investigation found that the original legal notices sent in the name of the RSS were also part of an apparent hoax. The investigation traced the address and phone number mentioned in those notices to another organisation, Rashtriya Seva Sangh, whose president denied sending them.

The two developments now establish that both the original notices sent in the RSS's name and the subsequent takedown requests attributed to Delhi Police were not authentic.

text:
Most interesting cultural takeaways from Mumbai, India

1. The culture on supporting women is so strong & unbelievably more left than we make it out in the west

The streets are literally plastered with ads saying #menwillbemen & every security check (entering malls or thru airport etc) has a separate women only line where the officer checks you inside a curtained box

2. They don't drink iced cold water

The water served at restaurants was always uncomfortably room temperature, even when I asked for it iced they would put a single ice cube in it. I also didn't see a single local get anything iced and if it was an iced drink they would ask them to remove the ice

3. Way more people speak English than I would have expected (unlike Buenos Aires... lol)

Mostly lower blue collar workers could only speak Hindi (some small street side vendors, security guards, janitors, etc). The guys that owned small storefronts could all speak perfectly & were incredible salesmen too

4. Legal drinking age is 25

I didn't drink at all the entire trip & idk how strongly this is enforced but that's 4 yrs more than any other country I've ever been to (Dubai & Indonesia are both 21), and we out here complaining about 21 in the US

5. Sidewalks & crosswalks don't exist

There's no coordinated mechanism for when to cross, it's just playing crossy road every day and u gotta send it. Reminds me of Indonesia, the drivers are all trained to stop within 2 ft of distance so it's fine

Overall was very reminiscent of Bangkok, super busy streets & even worse traffic, lots of cute cafes & beautiful luxurious malls
