ICYMI: The Day The Director of Forensic Services in Uganda Police, ACP Andrew Mubiru Told Court That The Results Before Court Were Edited and Not The Actual Results The Analysis System Produced. 

The defense called them “doctored”, he called them “edited” and said there was a reason for the editing, which he never provided. 

He also declined to provide the original form of the results, edit history or validation studies for independent verification as well; calling them “confidential”. 

I’m not making this up, read on for details.

I’ll explain in a three part series but first, the broad details;

In September 2024, during cross-examination by defence attorney Mr Elison Karuhanga, the Director of Forensics at @PoliceUg, Mr Andrew Kizimula Mubiru, was asked about the DNA electropherograms (EPGs) he had placed before court.

He said he was the analyst and he edited them. When asked for the originals, he said they were “confidential”. You might recall from our earlier reports that Mr Mubiru later denied being the analyst

Why this matters:

EPGs are computer generated graphs that display raw data produced during DNA separation and analysis. Reading them against a reference sample tells you how many people’s DNA is present, whose it is etc. Editing some peaks out cleverly hides this information.

The state's DNA report says a bed sheet recovered from Mrs Molly Katanga carried a single person's DNA profile, hers.

But the system's own match report, which Mr Mubiru attached as Annex 3, said otherwise. It flagged the bed sheet as a MIXTURE. At two DNA markers (D8S1179 and D7), the system recorded three alleles. Three alleles means at least two people.

The electropherograms before court showed only two alleles.

Asked where the third peak went, Mr Mubiru said it was a "stutter", a small artefact of the DNA copying process, and that he had removed it on review.

Mr Karuhanga asked him to show the stutter on the electropherogram.

He said: "It's not displayed”

EK: "So this is an edited electropherogram."

AM: "Yes, I edited."

He later conceded that, according to the system, the bed sheet "indicates a mixture… more than one person's DNA on it."

And when asked for the raw data and internal validation studies that would let anyone check his call? "The original data is available, but it's confidential."

Note: Removing stutter can be legitimate. Labs do it. But a stutter and a second person's DNA can look EXACTLY alike on a graph. The decision to call a peak "stutter" can turn a two-person mixture into a single-source profile. In a murder trial, that can be the whole case.

Mr Mubiru just invited court to not check him; but take his word for it; a courtroom version of “trust me bro”. 

He edited the graphs, set thresholds that didn’t match his own testimony, then held the raw data as "confidential". 

He invited court to ditch the science and instead trust him.

The Defense’s View

Mr Karuhanga called the police forensics lab “a kitchen that cooks results”.

Fast forward to July 2026;

Defense DNA expert Ms Lynne Hingley (DW4) told court:

1-Mr Mubiru said they used a threshold of 300 RFUs to remove noise (edit). The state's own software report shows 70. (See here: https://t.co/Hh3TUGnrAM)

2-A negative control contained DNA from at least 2 people, "a gross contamination event."

3-One gun sample with 4 contributors was modelled as if it had 3. The model then failed validation checks 7 times.

4-Even with perfect results, "the DNA result itself does not help address in any way who fired that gun."

On the issue of who was the analyst anyway? 

Mr Mubiru answered that. Well, sort of….

On different days, he described himself as the analyst, the lead examiner, the supervisor, "supervisor, not examiner," and the reviewer. 

He also told court the logged-in users were ASP Barnabas Haririmana and SP Lillian Mutesi, not himself. (See here: https://t.co/X40FfMb160)

You can find the cross-examination link here: https://t.co/sqSO9eIQyw

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.

From Hitchhikes to Hydrogen: A Day at India Energy Week - IEW 2024

Last minute, I decided to go to India Energy Week in Goa after finding out some industry acquaintances were attending.

I wasn't sure how to get there since the venue was in a remote place. I thought it wouldn't be too difficult, just take a bus to Goa and figure out the rest when I arrived. 

So, that's what I did. 

I took an overnight sleeper bus that dropped me off in Madgaon. Madgaon is an unassuming town, quite far from Goa's popular tourist spots. The venue was about 25 km further in a small village called Betul. The only way to get there was by local buses, so I took one to Betul. 

After arriving, I realized I still had a couple of kilometers to go to the venue, which was on a mountain near the town. The road was full of private cars going to the event, and it looked like it would take at least an hour to get through the traffic. So, I found a local bike rider, gave him 100 rupees, and asked him to drop me at the venue. He agreed to help me out.

When I arrived at the venue, I was really impressed. It was ONGC's training center, a huge, well-developed facility that could be compared to Houston's Reliant Center, although it doesn't have a stadium. 

There were 3 large halls with 300+ booths. Big Indian oil and gas companies and international majors occupied some of the large booths, but many were of modest size, used by OEMs and support service vendors.

Working in the LNG sector, I wasn't sure what to expect. India isn't a major buyer of LNG yet, and beyond its use in the fertilizer industry, LNG hasn't significantly penetrated other gas-consuming sectors in the country. 

I was curious to see which companies were marketing themselves at Energy Week and to gauge the overall energy sentiment from their presence. I definitely got a good overview.

Met people from various industry segments, including biofuel, battery technology, LPG trading, regas terminal operations, and commodity tracking. The representation of industries at the event was quite balanced.

One interesting encounter was with a young engineer from a company that builds turnkey biogas plants. He was very knowledgeable about the market. The government is supporting biogas strongly, as it helps reduce gas imports and encourages local production and consumption of gas. Companies get financial incentives based on how much gas they produce. 

He talked about a recent project where they approached a distillery to build a biogas plant using the distillery's waste. The plant is now operational and produces a significant amount of gas, enough to justify the investment. 

The process involves dumping several tons of waste into a digester tank every day, which then produces methane over a 27-day cycle. As the volume increases, it displaces the generated biogas, which is then cleaned of impurities and compressed to meet gas delivery standards for consumption. 

At the exhibition hall, I first walked to Baker Hughes booth and got hold of their technical experts of the turbine division.  

Wanted to find out how difficult it is to reprogram loading conditions for a turbine designed for a different liquefaction technology. Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project has that problem now. BH tested their LM-9000 turbines for the Linde process in 2020 and now Novatek has to reprogram those turbines to fit their new Arctic Cascade modified LNG liquefaction technology, as both Linde and BH have backed off from the project since the sanctions were in place from 2022. 

To put it in simple words, it is going to take a lot of trial and error to make the process work without making any modifications to the turbine's design. 

Each turbine is designed to suit a unique firing pattern associated with the loading of each section of the turbine chambers, usually, such process change means sending the turbine back to the vendor and having them redesign the affected parts of it such as impellers, blades etc. 

Now Novatek has to do this in-house. It is going to be a nightmare. If the turbines as not designed properly to suit the needs of the new process, they may develop hot spots in certain areas of the combustion chamber and can have irreversible damage. The way to avoid this without making physical alterations is to reduce the production capacity. 

Then I  visited Yokogawa booth, it is a big name company known for developing DCS and control systems for LNG facilities. I was eager to learn from their experts about the challenges Freeport LNG was encountering with its electric drive system. 

Specifically, I wondered if there were any inherent disadvantages from a control system standpoint. However, the insights I received were quite unexpected. 

Contrary to my assumption that electric drives might be more challenging to control compared to gas turbines, the experts told me that the control system's design wasn't the issue. Instead, the unconventional electric drive design approach adopted by Freeport LNG was the problem. 

The experts questioned the rationale behind deviating from conventional designs, especially when the anticipated benefits of electrification might not be fully realized. 

 Freeport LNG had abandoned a proven design, responsible for producing hundreds of millions of tons of LNG, in favor of a novel, electrically-driven approach aimed at satisfying environmentalist groups. But Freeport LNG has to face some serious challenges of motor failures - a setback their counterparts have clearly avoided as they continue to export LNG using the traditional design. 

This scenario suggested a disconnect where management may have overlooked the engineering team's advice, opting for an "environmentally friendly" label at the potential cost of operational stability.

Next, I made my way to several regasification terminal booths to gauge their current operations and future expansion plans. A significant hurdle they all highlighted was the insufficient pipeline infrastructure, which restricts the efficient distribution of gas to end-users. 

Beyond its application in the fertilizer industry, the majority of gas converted from LNG at these regas terminals is transported by trucks which falls short in terms of efficiency for broader distribution. 

Recently India has been working on an LNG export deal with Sri Lanka where the LNG will be transported via ships. I found out that it would be transported via LNG ISO containers and not by dedicated ships. 

S&P Global commodity insights group had a booth. Learned a lot of things from them. the company was operating under the name S&P Global Platts and recently merged with IHS Markit. Now they are the biggest name in commodity insights and pricing benchmarks for crude, gas and other commodities. Their Indian office is self-sustaining and does all the work of pricing benchmarks for the Indian market. The staff was knowledgeable and very professional. 

Met an LPG distributor who had a large distribution network in south India. Asked him about his business. Wanted to know if he sees PNG displacing the Urban LPG market anytime soon. He mentioned that in some major urban markets, the LPG growth has slowed down from double digits to single digits, but it hasn't reversed yet and is unlikely to do so for many years. 

Both CNG and LPG markets will continue to grow in urban areas. The distribution of PNG remains a big challenge in the urban markets as they are densely populated and to bring the distribution grid to support the population in those areas is a very difficult task. LPG will still dominate as cooking fuel in India and will see single-digit growth in urban markets and double-digit growth in rural markets. 

Met a few people who are taking an entrepreneurial interest in investing in alternative fuels. 

A bright young fella wanted to establish an RNG filling station network in a rural area where CNG is expensive to transport as there are no distribution lines, all the gas has to be transported via trucks. He wanted to gather agricultural waste from the neighboring farmers and run an RNG fueling station to support the growing number of CNG car users. 

Another gentleman was working on a battery prototype that would reduce the imports from China and could be made in India. 

Both were aware of the government programs that would offer significant cash incentives to these kinds of projects.  

As the day was wrapping up, had a chance to meet with Stephen Stapczynski, the LNG reporter for Bloomberg. I have been following him for many years and his reporting on the industry is top-notch. His news articles provide the best information about the latest happenings in the LNG industry and I always go to them as my primary source of what is happening in the LNG world.  

Amongst many things we discussed, one thing we both agreed on is how little public awareness is there about the LNG industry and wished more people knew about what was happening and would take interest in discussions on X. A lot of things are happening in this industry and most are going without notice or any serious interests from people at large. 

Most booths were staffed by key personnel who were engaging in serious dialogue with the visitors. Met many SME engineers and spoke at length with them on many issues, I felt right at home with them, as I was one of them in my past life. We talked shop, made connections, and some invited me for a conference call to introduce to their colleagues, it was a very enjoyable experience. 

In one of the exhibition halls, booths dedicated to different countries were closely grouped. Notably, despite recent tensions between the two nations concerning energy trade, the German booth was positioned directly opposite the Russian booth. This arrangement seemed unintentional, likely an oversight during the layout planning. Interestingly, the professionals at both booths appeared unfazed by this proximity. The irony of the situation was amusing. I had a chuckle while I was passing by noticing it. 

I attended a panel discussion. Spent about 20 minutes and then decided to leave. Most talk was about how the government is paying attention to this sector but not to that sector, and how methane leaks are a major problem, on and on. It was a gripe session. Didnt think I learned anything new from it. I get more information on such things on X-platform on a regular basis from people who seem to be more in tune with such challenges. May be Ipicked the most boring session of all. 

The event was well organized by DMG events, and very professionally set up and structured. Was pleasantly surprised by the presence of espresso machines making gourmet coffees at every major booth along with a selection of pastries and snacks.

The food scene was good. the cafeteria had many exotic alternatives and great local cuisine options were available along with the usual comfort foods from American fast food joints. Your boy settled for Domino's pizza & diet Pepsi (watching calories). Old habits die hard. 

The return trip turned out to be far more eventful than the one that kicked it off. On my way back from a mountaintop venue to the village of Betul at its base, I opted for a lift on a two-wheeler, planning afterward to catch a private car to the Madgaon bus station. 

I offered the bike rider a hundred rupees, but he declined the money, insisting I still join him. He revealed he was a police officer and couldn't accept the cash. I assured him it wasn't a bribe; I merely wanted to offer something for his kindness. He was in plain clothes, after all. 

Understanding my intention, and learning I was headed to Madgaon, he went out of his way to drop me off further along, closer to my destination. He was a true gentleman. 

At this new spot, I ran into another person from the exhibition, also on his way to Madgaon. We split a cab fare and reached our destination together. From there, I boarded a sleeper coach to my town, Pune.

The adventure didn't end there. 

At a morning rest stop, I took a little too long, and the bus departed without me, leaving my laptop and clothes onboard. Thankfully, I had my cellphone and quickly contacted the travel company, who managed to coordinate with the next bus to assist me. I hopped on the next bus. The bus captain from my original bus met me near the city with my belongings in hand. Although the ordeal seemed needless, it fortunately ended well - I didn't lose any luggage.

Attending India Energy Week in Goa on a whim proved to be an enlightening experience. It was filled with unexpected encounters and valuable insights into the energy sector. 
The event offered a comprehensive view of the current landscape and future directions of the Indian energy industry.

Insights from the event 

Many themes emerged while I spoke with other companies and eventgoers. I am listing them here.

Insight #1: The emphasis on renewable energy was evident across all booths. Every company, including those in the oil and gas sector, displayed their green product offerings. Notably, one oil company showcased an electrolyzer alongside a hydrogen-fired generator set that operates on a mix of diesel and hydrogen.

Insight #2: When I introduced myself as someone in the LNG industry, the first question I got was - What do you think about hydrogen? If I had a dime for every time someone asked this question, I could have retired by the time I left the venue. People somehow have put too much faith in the green hydrogen potential than in gas or LNG. Somehow everyone is hoping that India will jump directly to hydrogen use from coal without first transitioning to gas. I found that very amusing because these were some of the smartest people in the industry gathered there and they still were mostly unaware about challenges in the mass-scale adoption of hydrogen. 

Insight #2: Identifying myself as a professional in the LNG industry often led to the immediate question, "What do you think about hydrogen?" If I had received a dime for every time this question was asked, I could have retired by the end of the event. There appears to be a significant overestimation of green hydrogen's potential over gas or LNG. Many seem to hope that India will skip transitioning to gas and leap directly to hydrogen from coal. The industry professionals were largely unaware of the challenges associated with mass-scale hydrogen adoption. 

Insight #3: While the hype for hydrogen was palpable, the practical applications were non-existent. Upon my querying, I quickly found out that all of these were conceptual working models but they haven't been employed in actual use. Mainly because hardly anyone in India is currently producing green hydrogen. So I consider all these green hydrogen projects as "pilot projects".  

Insight # 4: Sustainable growth in the oil and gas field was the predominant theme. Everyone was promoting it and everyone was talking about it. I thought about it. Why is sustainability being so pushed so hard? Then I realized that India needs to step up its alternative fuel scene. There is way too much demand for all types of hydrocarbon-based fuels, and unless the local industry is not incentivized by investing in hydrocarbon alternatives, then most of that demand has to be filled with expensive imports. It is going to drain the government coffers of foreign exchange and the price tag for such imports can put a serious burden on end users. Sustainability is not just a buzzword for India's energy sector, it is a requirement of the time as it would be a deterrent to unchecked growth in hydrocarbon consumption. 

Insight #5: India's inability to achieve self-sufficiency in hydrocarbon production is evident due to insufficient oil and gas reserves for national energy security. Nonetheless, the country can expand its ethanol, biogas, RNG, solar, and battery technology sectors, reducing reliance on oil and gas imports—a focus of the current government, which encourages alternative energy production and entrepreneurial ventures in this area. It still leaves a lot of room for LNG imports as the magnitude of coal consumption is astonishingly high and the extent of sustainable initiatives will have minor influence on the demand. 

Insight #6: Discussions at the booths did not revolve around increasing LNG imports or drilling more oil and gas wells, despite these being core activities of the Indian energy industry. The emphasis was on promoting alternative energies rather than showcasing existing capabilities.

Insight #7: There was a significant presence of foreign companies in every energy industry. India's energy demand is being noticed and everyone wants a piece of the action. 

Insight #8: The lack of a developed pipeline grid is a major bottleneck affecting the prospects of future LNG trade with India. The proponents of hydrogen should be aware that such infrastructure needs to exist if hydrogen has the potential if not for complete replacement (pipe dream) then for blending into gas that it would be a deterrent for that too. 

Insight # 9: India's strategy of developing biomethane, ethanol, etc. is an indication of the government's focus on reducing hydrocarbon imports and is an important element in India's energy security. While India is constrained by the lack of oil and gas reserves to meet its hydrocarbon needs, there is no constraint presently over how much sustainable energy from domestic sources can be developed. 

Insight #10: Every form of energy has its place in India and is experiencing growth at an unprecedented level. Be it from renewable sources or hydrocarbon sources. Meeting the higher demand for energy to support economic growth has opened up Indian markets for all the energy suppliers around the world. 

Insight #11:  Even among the knowledgeable attendees of the exhibition, there was a lack of awareness about LNG's potential to replace dirtier fuels like coal and diesel. There was a noticeable preference for hydrogen as the future fuel, overlooking the slow but steady increase in LNG consumption and the current state of hydrogen adoption.

🚨🇮🇳 ARUNACHAL PRADESH: UPPER SIANG DAM, FOREIGN FUNDING & INDIA'S NATIONAL SECURITY

Most Indians are unaware of the strategic battle unfolding in Arunachal Pradesh.

🇨🇳 1. CHINA'S MEGA DAM

China launched construction of its 60,000-MW hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet in July 2025.

The river enters India as the Siang and becomes the Brahmaputra.

India has legitimate concerns about upstream water control, flooding and water security.

🇮🇳 2. INDIA'S RESPONSE

The Modi government is pursuing the proposed 11,200-MW Upper Siang Multipurpose Project.

Its objectives include hydropower generation, strategic water storage and potential flood moderation.

This is not merely an electricity project. It has significant implications for India's strategic preparedness in the Northeast.

🚨 3. CBI FOREIGN-FUNDING INVESTIGATION

The CBI registered an FIR on August 20, 2026, involving activist and lawyer Bhanu Tatak.

According to the allegations:
• ₹20.94 lakh in foreign-exchange transactions between 2022 and 2025.
• Funds allegedly received without mandatory FCRA authorisation.
• Tatak is associated with SIFF and Dibang Resistance.

Four overseas organisations identified in reporting:

1. Asia Indigenous Peoples Network on Extractive Industries and Energy – Philippines.
2. Indigenous Peoples Rights International – Philippines.
3. Front Line Defenders – Ireland.
4. Business and Human Rights Resource Centre – UK.

🔥 4. OCTOBER 23 VIOLENCE & POLICE ACTION

Following the anti-dam agitation in Pasighat:

• 26 people were apprehended, including five juveniles.
• Eight criminal cases were registered.
• An NHPC office and police station were attacked.
• Vehicles and public infrastructure were damaged.
• Political representatives' residences were reportedly vandalised.

Individuals named in police-related reporting include Ebo Mili, Otul Jerang and others.

Four activists detained under APUAPA were released on November 7:

• Adum Tayom
• Omak Paron
• Okut Paloh
• Oson Paron

The release was described by the government as a goodwill gesture to facilitate dialogue.

5. ORGANISATIONS IN THE ANTI-DAM MOVEMENT

SIFF, Dibang Resistance, SIFF Youth Wing, SAAYA and other local organisations have opposed the projects, citing indigenous rights, displacement and environmental concerns.

Peaceful opposition is a democratic right. Violence and alleged financial violations must be investigated separately.

🇮🇳 THE BIGGER QUESTION

China is building massive infrastructure upstream. India cannot afford to ignore the strategic implications.

The government must:
✔ Investigate alleged illegal foreign funding.
✔ Establish accountability for violence.
✔ Protect indigenous rights.
✔ Ensure fair rehabilitation and environmental safeguards.
✔ Strengthen India's water and border security.

National security, environmental responsibility and the rights of Arunachal's people must go together.

India's strategic interests on the Brahmaputra deserve a serious national debate.

Imagine this: last February, I filed a police report regarding a cyberattack on my private network. Just 14 days later, I received a notice from the public prosecutor’s office stating, "Perpetrators could not be identified." 

This was happening at the same time as "Operation Endgame"—a major, large-scale investigation led by the BKA and Europol. I had observed all the specific indicators on my own hardware and included them in my report. 

I also provided the motive behind the destruction of my server—a RAID 6 setup with an LSI RAID controller that suffered three hard drive failures in a single week, even though I replaced the faulty drives immediately—and the compromise of my devices: "the theft of sensitive scientific research." 

This makes perfect sense, of course, when your own private IP shows up as the first hop in a traceroute, and the target addresses you’re trying to reach all point back to that same IP. 

Last year, the systems on Cloudflare weren't quite as advanced, but thanks to the "kind assistance" of a certain AI—one whose name ends in "OK"—everything has become much more professional. Not perfect yet, perhaps, but certainly better. 

Would you blindly trust an AI whose name ends in "OK"?

text:
KNOW YOUR RIGHTS: WHEN THE POLICE COME TO YOUR DOOR, KNOW THE LAW BEFORE YOU PANIC

Police authority is necessary for public safety. But no police officer is above the Constitution. Every citizen has rights, every search has legal safeguards, and every arrest must follow due process.

The video raises an important public-interest issue: ordinary citizens often do not know what to do when police officers arrive at their homes, seek questioning, conduct searches or attempt to take someone into custody.

Fear, confusion and lack of legal awareness can make people vulnerable to intimidation or procedural violations.

The answer is not to obstruct lawful police work. It is to understand the law, cooperate lawfully and insist that constitutional safeguards are respected.

SOURCE AND SCOPE

The supplied video recommends four basic precautions: ask for written notice when summoned for questioning, document the interaction, ask for search authorisation, and ensure independent witnesses and video recording during a search.

These recommendations contain useful advice, but some need legal qualification. India's current criminal procedure law is the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, effective from 1 July 2024. The following SOP explains what the law actually requires.

WHEN POLICE SEEK TO QUESTION YOU

Under Section 179 BNSS, an investigating officer may require a person acquainted with a case to attend by written order.

Importantly, women, males below 15 or above 60, persons with disabilities and persons with acute illness cannot be required to attend anywhere other than their residence. They may voluntarily agree to attend the police station. IndiaCode +1

Section 180 permits police questioning, but a person cannot be compelled to answer questions whose answers may expose them to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture.

Section 181 provides that a statement made to police during investigation, if reduced to writing, must not be signed by the person making it, subject to statutory exceptions. Do not sign blank papers or documents you have not read. IndiaCode +1

WHEN POLICE WANT TO SEARCH YOUR HOME

Do not assume that every search requires a warrant. The law recognises certain warrantless searches.

Under Section 185 BNSS, an investigating officer may conduct a search without a warrant when statutory conditions are satisfied. The officer must record the grounds in the case diary and specify, as far as possible, what is being sought.

The search must be video-recorded. Relevant records must reach the Magistrate within 48 hours, and the occupant can apply for a free copy. IndiaCode +1

Under Section 103:

* Two or more independent local witnesses should be called to witness the search.

* A list of seized articles and their locations must be prepared and signed by witnesses.

* The occupant or their representative must be allowed to remain present.

* A copy of the signed seizure list must be provided.

* A woman's personal search must be conducted by another woman, with due regard to decency. IndiaCode +1

Section 105 separately mandates audio-video recording of the search and seizure process, including preparation of the seizure list and witnesses' signatures. IndiaCode

IF THE POLICE ARREST SOMEONE

Section 35 regulates arrest without warrant. Where arrest is not necessary under the statutory conditions, police must issue a notice to appear. Compliance ordinarily protects the person from arrest in that case unless reasons for arrest are subsequently recorded. IndiaCode

Sections 36, 38, 47 and 48 provide safeguards concerning identification of arresting officers, arrest documentation, access to an advocate during interrogation, communication of grounds of arrest and informing a nominated relative or friend. IndiaCode +1

Article 22(2) of the Constitution requires production of an arrested person before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding necessary journey time. Ministry of External Affairs +1

THE CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLE

In Joginder Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1994), the Supreme Court made an essential distinction: the legal power to arrest does not automatically justify exercising it. Arrest cannot be routine. SCI API +1

The Supreme Court's D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) guidelines also established safeguards against arbitrary arrest and custodial abuse. SCI API +1

WHAT CITIZENS SHOULD DO

Remain calm. Verify police identification. Ask for the legal basis of the visit. Request copies of notices, warrants and seizure lists where applicable. Document events without obstructing lawful duties. Contact a lawyer or trusted person. If safeguards are violated, preserve evidence and approach the appropriate senior police authority, Magistrate, State Human Rights Commission or court.

THE BIGGER ISSUE

A democracy cannot ask citizens to surrender their constitutional rights out of fear of the police. Nor can it expect police officers to function without lawful authority.

The Constitution protects citizens, regulates state power and demands accountability from every public authority.

Know your rights. Respect lawful authority. Never confuse obedience to the law with submission to intimidation.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Fake court orders how? Why? Top 10.

As per Reuters, DoT got 129 websites blocked on two fake High Court orders. Last week X told the Delhi HC that the Delhi Police orders against IFF were fake too.

1. Too many censorship bodies. MeitY, MHA, MIB, DoT, state governments, police and courts all issue takedown or blocking orders.

2. Too many censorship laws. 69A, 79(3)(b), IT Rules, BNSS notices, court orders, each with its own format, so nobody knows what a real order should look like. The Sahyog platform by templatisation has only automated the process, not made the orders intelligible. 

3. Pressure on platforms to act immediately, even pre-censor. The deadline is three hours and nobody can verify an order in that time.

4. No one to check, just censor. DoT got a fake High Court order on email on a Sunday night and told ISPs to block 34 sites two days later. It was not even on the court's website. Our government is incompetent and trigger happy to take down even global web services. Full domain and app blocking is now a norm. 

5. Notices have no legal threshold and rely on subjective perception of offence and vibez. A fake one reads the same as a real one. What’s fact or fiction when our censorship regime is based on magic realism. 

6. MeitY is incompetent and can only pressure Silicon Valley platforms to take down more and faster. Ask who issued an order and it says not us. It does not want to provide statistics, shies away from transparency and every six months gets the itch to amend the IT Rules, 2021. 

7. Courts pass John Doe and dynamic injunctions so often that lawyers emailing DoT a new list of sites to block is normal. One more email from an "advocate" is not sus to anyone.

8. Orders are kept secret. The person censored rarely gets a copy so they can't say it is fake. We found out only because X forwarded the notices to us, and Reuters because DoT puts court orders online (this category is a rare exception). 

9. Platforms are punished only for not complying. Ignore a real order and you lose safe harbour and staff can be prosecuted. Obey a fake one and nothing happens lol.

10. Much of this is automated. Meta reportedly acts on government flags without human review and I4C says it has no record of notices sent through Sahyog.

Quite simply, censorship is the norm and speech is put to suspicion.

India’s government ordered blocking of 100+ illegal betting websites based on two court orders. But @Reuters has found the court orders were fake. 

The two court orders carried blue court seals, a fake QR code and made-up case numbers such as “Writ - A 30480/2026”. They were sent by individuals who claimed to be lawyers, and asked for immediate implementation by Indian government.
